# Education in Greece
Education in Greece comprises a structured system starting with compulsory preschool education at ages 4–6 (Pre-kindergarten and Kindergarten), followed by six years of primary school (Dimotiko) for ages 6–12. Upon completion, students automatically enroll in Gymnasium, the compulsory lower secondary school lasting three years for ages 12–15. Upper secondary education, known as Lyceum, is non-compulsory, lasting three years (ages 15–18), culminating in the awarding of the Apolytirio Lykeiou diploma, which is required for higher education admission. Greek students begin learning English in kindergarten, emphasizing early foreign language acquisition.
The education system includes various specialized institutions such as Vocational High Schools (EPAL), Experimental Vocational Schools, and Adult Second Chance Schools, offering both general and vocational training aligned with European qualification frameworks. Vocational programs provide dual diplomas and pathways to higher education. Higher education consists of autonomous public and private universities, with tuition-free access for most students; English-taught programs and private colleges that collaborate with foreign universities also exist. Greece’s qualification framework (HQF) aligns with European standards, covering from primary through tertiary levels, incorporating formal and non-formal education. Non-formal education includes online courses, lifelong learning centers, and public training initiatives. Despite the structured system, education in Greece faces challenges such as corruption in public education, past practices of school corporal punishment (now banned), and incidents of student bullying, reflecting ongoing social concerns within the sector.
